hints.title: Make a table of terms
hints.body: Use columns for n, f(n) and g(n). Apply the rule according to whether the current value is odd or even.
hints.recap: The parity of the current term chooses the next rule.
hints.pitfall: An odd index does not necessarily mean an odd term.
hints.pause: Continue until you see a repeated value in each sequence.

recall.reminder: The parity of the current term chooses the next rule.

hints.title: Mark where each repeat starts
hints.body: Check that the repeated value is followed by the same updates. Mark the first index of each repeating block and its length.
hints.recap: The first few terms may lie outside the repeating block.
hints.pitfall: Do not count the non-repeating start as part of the cycle.
hints.pause: Record the start and length of each cycle.

recall.reminder: The first few terms may lie outside the repeating block.

hints.title: Count from the start of the cycle
hints.body: For each sequence, subtract its cycle-start index from 1000. Divide by the cycle length and use the remainder to move along the block.
hints.recap: Whole cycles return to the same position.
hints.pitfall: The two sequences may have different cycle lengths.
hints.pause: Find both terms at index 1000 and subtract in the stated order.

recall.reminder: Whole cycles return to the same position.

solution:
For f, the terms are 5,16,8,4,2,1,4,2,1,… . The rule sends 4→2→1→4, so this three-term block repeats from index 4. As 1000−4=996=3×332, f(1000)=4.

For g, the terms are 3,8,4,2,1,6,3,… . The rule returns 6 to 3, so the six-term block repeats from index 1. Since 1000=6×166+4, g(1000)=2.

Therefore f(1000)−g(1000)=4−2=2.

Answer D.
knowledgePattern: Find eventual cycles of two parity-dependent recurrences
